translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
tafsir_summary: The Basmala opens every chapter of the Quran and every righteous action. Ibn Kathir explains that beginning with Allah's name invokes His blessings and acknowledges that all acts derive their value from His permission. Al-Tabari notes that 'Rahman' (الرحمن) denotes the vastness of divine mercy encompassing all creation, while 'Raheem' (الرحيم) denotes the specific mercy reserved for believers. Al-Qurtubi adds that reciting this phrase is an act of worship that aligns the servant's intention with the divine will.

translation: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all the worlds.
tafsir_summary: This verse establishes that all praise belongs exclusively to Allah. Ibn Kathir explains that 'al-hamd' encompasses gratitude and praise for both outward and inward blessings. 'Rabb al-'alamin' (Lord of the worlds) means He is the Creator, Sustainer, and Master of every realm — humans, jinn, angels, and all unseen creation. Al-Tabari notes this verse teaches that praising Allah should be instinctive, arising from recognizing His lordship over everything we experience.

translation: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.
tafsir_summary: This is the central declaration of monotheism in Surah Al-Fatiha. Ibn Kathir notes the grammatical inversion ('You alone' before the verb) emphasizes exclusivity — worship and help-seeking are directed to Allah alone, no other. Al-Qurtubi explains this verse as the covenant between the servant and Allah: worship combines love, fear, and hope together. Al-Tabari says 'isti'ana' (seeking help) acknowledges human weakness and that true power belongs only to Allah.

arabic: ذَٰلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ
translation: This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those conscious of Allah.
tafsir_summary: Ibn Kathir explains 'la rayba fihi' (no doubt in it) as an absolute negation — the Quran's divine origin, completeness, and guidance are beyond question. The guidance it contains is specifically for 'al-muttaqin', those who have taqwa: consciousness of Allah that leads to obedience and avoidance of disobedience. Al-Tabari notes that taqwa is the prerequisite for benefiting from the Quran's guidance, as a heart turned toward Allah receives its light.

arabic: وَاسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ ۚ وَإِنَّهَا لَكَبِيرَةٌ إِلَّا عَلَى الْخَاشِعِينَ
translation: And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humbly submissive to Allah.
tafsir_summary: This verse pairs sabr (patience) with salah (prayer) as the two primary means of seeking Allah's help through trials. Ibn Kathir explains that sabr covers patience in acts of obedience, patience in avoiding sin, and patience with divine decree. Al-Qurtubi notes that salah is described as 'heavy' for the heedless because they lack khushu' (humble focus), but light for those who experience the prayer as meeting with their Lord. Al-Tabari adds that the combination teaches that inner patience and outer worship reinforce each other.

arabic: فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ وَاشْكُرُوا لِي وَلَا تَكْفُرُونِ
translation: So remember Me; I will remember you. And be grateful to Me and do not deny Me.
tafsir_summary: This verse contains a divine promise: remembering Allah draws His remembrance in return. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah's remembrance of the believer is manifested as praise before the angels, mercy, forgiveness, and guidance. Al-Tabari notes 'dhikr' includes prayer, supplications, reciting the Quran, and holding Allah's greatness in the heart. Al-Qurtubi adds that gratitude and remembrance are complementary — gratitude for blessings increases them, while ingratitude removes their barakah.

arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ
translation: O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.
tafsir_summary: Ibn Kathir notes this verse parallels 2:45 but is addressed specifically to believers, deepening its meaning. The divine company promised to the patient ('Allah is with the patient') is the company of aid, love, and special care — not just general omnipresence. Al-Tabari explains that sabr here encompasses all three forms: patience in worship, patience in abstaining from the forbidden, and acceptance of trials. Al-Qurtubi adds that salah reminds the believer of Allah's greatness and thereby makes the burden of patience lighter.

arabic: إِنَّ فِي خَلْقِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَاخْتِلَافِ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ لَآيَاتٍ لِّأُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ
translation: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding.
tafsir_summary: This verse calls people of intellect ('uli al-albab') to contemplate the universe as signs of Allah. Ibn Kathir explains that 'albab' (plural of lubb) refers to the pure, sound intellect that pierces through the superficial to the deeper meaning. The alternation of day and night points to the precision of divine design — regularity that sustains life, marking time and revealing the Creator's attributes of wisdom and power. Al-Tabari notes that this contemplation is an obligation, not merely an option, for those endowed with reason.

arabic: الَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ اللَّهَ قِيَامًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ وَيَتَفَكَّرُونَ فِي خَلْقِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ
translation: Those who remember Allah while standing or sitting or lying on their sides and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth.
tafsir_summary: Following 3:190, this verse describes the 'uli al-albab' — people of understanding — as those who combine continuous dhikr with tafakkur (deep reflection). Ibn Kathir explains that dhikr in all postures means the heart remains connected to Allah throughout all states of life. Al-Qurtubi notes that tafakkur in creation is a distinct form of worship, as it deepens the appreciation of divine attributes. Al-Tabari adds that the combination of heart-remembrance and intellectual reflection is the hallmark of true believers.

translation: Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.
tafsir_summary: One of the most cited verses on spiritual wellbeing. Ibn Kathir explains that 'tuma'ninah' (tranquility/rest) is the specific quality of the heart that has found certainty in Allah. This peace is not mere contentment but a deep settlement — the heart returns to its natural state of reliance on its Creator. Al-Tabari explains that dhikr here encompasses all forms: prayer, Quran recitation, supplication, and holding Allah's presence in consciousness. Al-Qurtubi notes that the verse implies that anxiety and restlessness are symptoms of disconnection from dhikr — the cure is a return to Allah's remembrance.

arabic: أَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِدُلُوكِ الشَّمْسِ إِلَىٰ غَسَقِ اللَّيْلِ وَقُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ ۖ إِنَّ قُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ كَانَ مَشْهُودًا
translation: Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of night and the recitation of dawn. Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.
tafsir_summary: This verse establishes the five daily prayers and highlights the special status of Fajr prayer. Ibn Kathir explains that the 'witnessed' nature of Fajr means both the angels of the night and the angels of the day are present during it, making it of exceptional spiritual weight. Al-Tabari notes that the structure of the verse — covering the full arc of the day — teaches that prayer is the backbone of the Muslim's day, anchoring time and consciousness. Al-Qurtubi adds that the Fajr Quran recitation (salah) is given special emphasis because it is recited in stillness, before the world's noise begins.

arabic: إِذْ أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ فَقَالُوا رَبَّنَا آتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةً وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًا
translation: When the youths retreated to the cave and said: Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us from our affair right guidance.
tafsir_summary: The opening of the People of the Cave story. Ibn Kathir explains that these young believers fled to the cave to preserve their faith from a corrupt society — their supplication combines two requests: mercy (rahmah) from Allah's side, and guidance (rashad) in their practical affairs. Al-Tabari notes this du'a is a model: acknowledge complete reliance on Allah, then ask for guidance in one's specific situation. Al-Qurtubi highlights that they 'withdrew' (awaw) seeking Allah, teaching that sometimes spiritual survival requires creating distance from what harms one's faith.

arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ ذِكْرًا كَثِيرًا
translation: O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance.
tafsir_summary: A direct divine command for abundant dhikr. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah commands 'dhikran kathiran' (much remembrance) without specifying a maximum — the call is to make remembrance a constant state, not a scheduled ritual. He contrasts this with other obligations that have defined times, emphasizing that dhikr has no limit. Al-Tabari explains that the command to believers specifically implies that dhikr is a mark of true faith and that neglecting it represents spiritual diminishment. Al-Qurtubi connects this to 13:28 — the peace of heart promised there is achieved through the abundant remembrance commanded here.

arabic: أَمَّنْ هُوَ قَانِتٌ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ سَاجِدًا وَقَائِمًا يَحْذَرُ الْآخِرَةَ وَيَرْجُو رَحْمَةَ رَبِّهِ
translation: Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord?
tafsir_summary: This verse describes the night-worshipper who balances fear and hope. Ibn Kathir explains that the contrast implied (with those who ignore worship) answers itself — of course the worshipping servant is superior. The night prayer (qiyam al-layl) is held in high esteem because it is voluntary, done in privacy, and represents sincere devotion without social recognition. Al-Qurtubi notes that the combination of 'fearing the Hereafter and hoping for mercy' defines the healthy spiritual state: neither despair nor delusion, but a balance that drives righteous action.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
tafsir_summary: This refrain, repeated 31 times in Surah Al-Rahman, is one of the most rhetorical and emotionally powerful patterns in the Quran. Ibn Kathir explains that the repetition is not redundancy but emphasis — each iteration follows a new description of divine blessings, and the question challenges humans and jinn to justify any denial. Al-Tabari notes that 'ala' (favors) covers material gifts, spiritual provisions, and the very capacity to perceive beauty. Al-Qurtubi says the frequency of the refrain is itself a mercy — Allah repeatedly reminds His servants of His generosity to cultivate gratitude and prevent heedlessness.

translation: Your Lord has not abandoned you, nor has He detested you.
tafsir_summary: Revealed during a period when Quranic revelation had paused, this verse was a direct reassurance to the Prophet (peace be upon him). Ibn Kathir explains that 'wada'a' means complete abandonment, and 'qala' means hatred or strong dislike — both are absolutely negated. This verse teaches that divine silence or apparent distance in trials does not mean abandonment. Al-Tabari notes it carries a universal message: Allah's love for His servant does not waver based on hardship or the pausing of visible signs. Al-Qurtubi adds that this ayah is recited in times of spiritual depression as a reminder of Allah's continuous care.

translation: For indeed, with hardship will be ease.
tafsir_summary: Repeated twice in Surah Al-Inshirah (94:5-6), this promise is one of the most comforting in the Quran. Ibn Kathir notes a grammatical insight from classical scholars: 'al-'usr' (the hardship) uses the definite article suggesting one specific hardship, while 'yusr' (ease) is indefinite — meaning one hardship can bring multiple forms of ease. Al-Tabari explains that 'ma'a' (with) not 'ba'd' (after) means ease is embedded within the hardship itself, not simply following it. Al-Qurtubi notes the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, 'One hardship cannot overcome two eases' — referring to its repetition in verses 5 and 6.

translation: Say: He is Allah, the One.
tafsir_summary: The opening verse of Surah Al-Ikhlas, which the Prophet (peace be upon him) described as equivalent in reward to one-third of the Quran. Ibn Kathir explains that 'Ahad' (One) is more absolute than 'Wahid' (single) — it denotes absolute uniqueness with no comparison, partner, or equal. Al-Tabari notes that the surah was revealed partly in response to those who asked about Allah's nature and lineage, and it answers with pure theological precision. Al-Qurtubi adds that reciting this surah consistently purifies the heart of subtle forms of shirk by grounding it in the truth of divine oneness.
